answer.answer:
Prefabrication rests on two requirements: precise up-front planning and logistics, and a regulatory and certification pathway for offsite compliance, with the planning burden by far the more widely felt of the two. Three further enablers put a project in a position to prefabricate at all: DfMA for DFAB process, early contractor involvement and integrating the supply chain, so most of what prefabrication needs is organisational rather than technical. All five links rest on peer-reviewed literature, none on a standard, and every claim below comes from that literature rather than from any deployed Japanese line, because no such case record is in front of me.

**What prefabrication itself requires**

Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) carries ten dependency links in total, four inbound and six outbound, and the list is complete, so these counts may be read as exact. Two of them are requirements in the strict sense:

- Rely on precise planning (RI14): prefabrication depends on precise up-front planning and logistics [1], peer-reviewed evidence (DEP33). RI14 is drawn on by 36 of the 50 coded cases, making it one of the most pervasive conditions in the whole record.
- Regulatory/legal concern (RI18): prefabrication depends on a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance, which requires third-party certification and traceability [2], peer-reviewed evidence (DEP96). RI18 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 coded cases, a third of RI14's reach, so the certification route bites in a much narrower set of projects than the planning demand does.

**What puts a project in a position to prefabricate**

Three enablers sit upstream of prefabrication and are what you build first:

- DfMA for DFAB process (PR9), because DfMA orients the project toward offsite manufacture [3] (DEP15, peer-reviewed). PR9 is drawn on by 15 of the 50 coded cases.
- Early contractor involvement (CO11), because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party, manufacturer, fabricator or contractor, to be involved in the early design phase, and a delivery method that brings participants into early design should be selected [4] (DEP22, peer-reviewed). CO11 is drawn on by 14 of the 50 coded cases.
- Integrate supply chain (VA14), where supply chain integration supports the offsite production line [5] (DEP79, peer-reviewed). VA14 is drawn on by 14 of the 50 coded cases.

**One direction worth reading carefully**

Robotic assembly (PR4) has prefabrication as a precondition, not the reverse: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [5] (DEP55, peer-reviewed). Prefabrication is the requirement on that edge, so it is upstream of robotic assembly, which is itself drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases.

**What prefabrication returns**

Four outbound enabling links, all peer-reviewed: offsite factory work compresses the schedule [6] (DEP17, VA2, drawn on by 49 of 50 cases), the controlled factory environment improves quality [7] (DEP18, VA3, 37 of 50), moving work offsite improves site safety [8] (DEP19, VA13, 39 of 50), and factory-based production improves quality control and reduces errors and rework [9] (DEP80, VA10, 19 of 50). Note that only the single path DEP19 runs from prefabrication to site safety.

**On evidence grade**

The graph holds eight dependency edges graded 'standard', listed in full [5], and prefabrication appears on none of them: the certification requirement on RI18 is carried by peer-reviewed work on offsite building-code compliance, not by a cited standard. Prefabrication/off-site is itself drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases. No deployed process record or firm is present in this context for prefabrication, so nothing above should be read as the behaviour of a specific production line.
